chapter: Pee Wee Russell and going solo
title: Never again for a bandleader: soloist years and the World's Greatest Jazz Band
summary: After Goodman Freeman vowed to be a soloist, survived lean years, and spent six years in a Colorado millionaire's band of soloists.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Managers, bookers and the business of getting work

blocks.x: So we, who thought we were going to escape into an easy life, found that we might have picked the most difficult life we could. But I am very happy that I got into it, because now I have things pretty much my own way. I have stopped -- when I left Benny Goodman, I vowed that I would never work again for another bandleader and I never have. I went out as a soloist and there were many lean years, and I just managed to survive and then I finally, I think the last band I played with, I am sure it was the last band I played with, was a band put together by a rich man from Colorado and it was an ideal setup, we were all paid very good salaries and we worked in the beginning a few months a year and then we were able to free-lance doing our other things.

I stayed with that thing for six years, because in that band, I was -- the band was built around ten soloists in the beginning and then went to nine and later to seven, and we had all the freedom we wanted. We could play -- I was there because I was a soloist. I could do anything I wanted. We made plenty of money. We had a very good way of life and we didn't work hard. There was a lot of traveling and a lot of sleep lost different days, but I -- we came to Europe a couple of times and I got a picture of London and the U.K. and
I wondered if I shouldn't try living in Europe for awhile and then I got a --
